title: 2 Samuel 7:18–29
context: 2 Samuel 7:18–29 is David’s prayer in response to Nathan’s oracle. David goes in and sits before the LORD, marveling at God’s grace to him and his house. He praises God’s greatness and uniqueness, recalls God’s redemption of Israel from Egypt, and asks God to confirm and fulfill his promise forever. The prayer is a model of humble, God-centered response to divine promise: it takes God’s word as the ground of its confidence and asks God to do what he has said. In the repeated address “Lord GOD,” “Lord” translates the Hebrew “Adonai.”

verses.text: Then David the king went in and sat before the LORD; and he said, “Who am I, Lord GOD, and what is my house, that you have brought me this far?
verses.arminianNotes: David sits before the LORD and asks, “Who am I, Lord GOD, and what is my house, that you have brought me this far?” “Lord” here translates “Adonai.” Arminian readers note David’s humility. He receives God’s promise not as his due but as undeserved grace, and his first response is wonder.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that David’s question confesses that all he has comes from God’s free grace. He brings nothing to the covenant but receives everything. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a model of humble response to God’s promise, in which the believer marvels that God should show such favor.

verses.text: This was yet a small thing in your eyes, Lord GOD, but you have spoken also of your servant’s house for a great while to come; and this among men, Lord GOD!
verses.arminianNotes: David says that what God has done was “a small thing in your eyes,” for God has spoken of David’s house “for a great while to come.” Arminian readers note that David recognizes the long reach of God’s promise, extending far beyond his own lifetime. The closing phrase, “and this among men,” is difficult, and the parallel in 1 Chronicles 17:17 words it differently.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David sees the promise as reaching into the distant future, which both traditions understand as finding its fulfillment in Christ. God’s generosity exceeds all expectation. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as David’s grateful recognition of the scope of God’s promise, while acknowledging that the final phrase is hard to render with certainty.

verses.text: What more can David say to you? For you know your servant, Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: “What more can David say to you? For you know your servant, Lord GOD.” Arminian readers note that David runs out of words. He rests in the knowledge that God knows him fully, a source of both humility and comfort in the relationship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God’s knowledge of David underlies the whole covenant. God chose and knew David before David knew God’s purposes. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an expression of trust in God’s intimate knowledge of his servant, and both see in it a pattern for believers’ prayer.

verses.text: For your word’s sake, and according to your own heart, you have worked all this greatness, to make your servant know it.
verses.arminianNotes: “For your word’s sake, and according to your own heart, you have worked all this greatness.” Arminian readers note that David grounds God’s actions in God’s own word and character. The covenant flows from who God is, not from David’s merit.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that God acts “according to your own heart,” from his own good pleasure and purpose. The source of the covenant lies wholly in God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as confessing that God’s grace originates in his own character and word, and that David is the recipient, not the cause, of the blessing.

verses.text: Therefore you are great, LORD God. For there is no one like you, neither is there any God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore you are great, LORD God. For there is no one like you, neither is there any God besides you.” Arminian readers note that David’s wonder at God’s promise leads to praise of God himself. The gift points to the Giver, and the right response to grace is to praise the God who gives it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David’s confession echoes Israel’s song at the sea, “Who is like you, LORD, among the gods?” (Exodus 15:11). God’s uniqueness is the foundation of Israel’s faith. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a confession of monotheism and of God’s incomparable greatness, the right center of all worship.

verses.text: What one nation on the earth is like your people, even like Israel, whom God went to redeem to himself for a people, and to make himself a name, and to do great things for you, and awesome things for your land, before your people, whom you redeemed to yourself out of Egypt, from the nations and their gods?
verses.arminianNotes: David asks, “What one nation on the earth is like your people,” whom God redeemed from Egypt to make himself a name. Arminian readers note that David places God’s promise to him within the larger story of God’s redemption of Israel. His own blessing is part of God’s purposes for his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the language of redemption, God going “to redeem to himself for a people,” emphasizes God’s initiative in choosing and saving Israel (compare Deuteronomy 4:34). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as celebrating God’s redemptive acts, which both see as foreshadowing the greater redemption in Christ.

verses.text: You established for yourself your people Israel to be your people forever; and you, LORD, became their God.
verses.arminianNotes: “You established for yourself your people Israel to be your people forever; and you, LORD, became their God.” Arminian readers note the covenant formula, “your people … their God,” which expresses the relationship God established with Israel and invites his people’s faithful response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the formula echoes God’s promise to Abraham “to be a God to you and to your offspring after you” (Genesis 17:7). The covenant with David continues the covenant with Abraham. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as affirming God’s lasting covenant relationship with his people, grounded in his own initiative.

verses.text: “Now, LORD God, the word that you have spoken concerning your servant, and concerning his house, confirm it forever, and do as you have spoken.
verses.arminianNotes: “Now, LORD God, the word that you have spoken … confirm it forever, and do as you have spoken.” Arminian readers note that David prays for what God has already promised. Prayer does not seek to change God’s purpose but to embrace it and ask for its fulfillment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David’s prayer is grounded entirely in God’s word: he asks God to do what God has said. God’s promises are the warrant and pattern for prayer. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a model of praying God’s promises back to him, with confidence that he will keep his word.

verses.text: Let your name be magnified forever, saying, ‘The LORD of Armies is God over Israel; and the house of your servant David will be established before you.’
verses.arminianNotes: “Let your name be magnified forever.” Arminian readers note that David’s concern is not only for his own house but for God’s glory. The establishment of David’s house will display God’s faithfulness and magnify his name among the nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that God’s glory is the ultimate goal of the covenant. David’s prayer for his house is subordinate to his desire for God’s name to be honored. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a God-centered prayer, joining the good of God’s people with the glory of his name.

verses.text: For you, LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, have revealed to your servant, saying, ‘I will build you a house.’ Therefore your servant has found in his heart to pray this prayer to you.
verses.arminianNotes: David says that because God revealed, “I will build you a house,” “your servant has found in his heart to pray this prayer.” Arminian readers note that God’s promise gives David boldness to pray. Revelation invites response, and confident prayer is the fitting answer to God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God’s word precedes and enables David’s prayer. The courage to pray comes from what God has first revealed. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that God’s promises are the foundation of bold prayer, and both see it as a pattern for believers who pray on the basis of God’s word.

verses.text: “Now, O Lord GOD, you are God, and your words are truth, and you have promised this good thing to your servant.
verses.arminianNotes: David prays, “you are God, and your words are truth, and you have promised this good thing to your servant.” Arminian readers note David’s confidence in the reliability of God’s word. Because God’s words are true, David can trust the promise fully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize the truthfulness of God’s words as the ground of covenant assurance. What God promises, he will do. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a confession of the truthfulness of God’s word, and both see in it a foundation for trusting all of God’s promises, fulfilled in Christ.

verses.text: Now therefore, let it please you to bless the house of your servant, that it may continue forever before you; for you, Lord GOD, have spoken it. Let the house of your servant be blessed forever with your blessing.”
verses.arminianNotes: David asks, “let it please you to bless the house of your servant, that it may continue forever before you; for you, Lord GOD, have spoken it.” Arminian readers note that David closes by asking for God’s blessing, resting his request on God’s spoken word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that David’s final petition, “Let the house of your servant be blessed forever with your blessing,” rests on God’s promise rather than on David’s worthiness. Shared ground: both traditions read the prayer’s conclusion as a model of confident, humble dependence on God’s word, and both see the eternal blessing fulfilled in Christ, the son of David.
